description: Hi, I am Rachel. I am interested in robotics and mechatronics. I hope to learn more about IOT and sensors design to connect embedded systems.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Ignis turns NASA’s two generations of fire satellites into one comparable record, then uses it to look ahead.

  1. Match: pair individual MODIS and VIIRS detections within adjustable distance and time limits, counting disagreement only where both sensors looked.
  2. Calibrate: put MODIS and Suomi NPP onto the NOAA-20 VIIRS scale, separately for each region and season.
  3. Validate: test every year with a model that never saw it. In Southeast Asia, accuracy is 0.96, and the 80% error band holds 79% of the time.
  4. Forecast: predict the next 26 weeks from recent fire, the El Niño index and NASA POWER rainfall, scored against a normal-year guess.

The website is a mission console covering 8 regions (Malaysia, Sumatra and Bornoe, Southeast Asia, India, Australia, Brazil, United State, Canada, Central Africa) worldwide:

  • Globe: a 3D globe with fire columns, country and province selection, and a 25-year timeline.
  • Live: this week ranked against every comparable week since 2001.
  • Fire Wire: a planet-wide live news strip.
  • Record: a burning calendar of every week since 2001.
  • Orbit: the satellites on their real orbits, with the real-time sun and true swath widths.
  • Pixels and Verify: why the sensors disagree, then proof that they agree.
  • Forecast: the outlook, predicted burning map, burn-window planner, season start and end, drought, and a haze outlook for Malaysia and Singapore.
  • Method: validation, limits, and CSV or JSON downloads for any date range.
  • Guided tour: explains every feature.

Benefits and impact

  • Fire and haze agencies: an early-warning view that compares this week with 25 years, plus a haze outlook.
  • Farmers and land managers: lower-risk burn windows they can add to a calendar.
  • Researchers: a downloadable, harmonized record with error bars.
  • The public: a clear explanation of why satellites disagree.

Tools: NASA FIRMS, LANCE, GIBS and POWER, plus the NOAA El Niño index and Natural Earth. Pipeline: Python (NumPy, pandas, Shapely). Website: TypeScript, React, MapLibre, three.js, d3. Live data runs through a Vercel serverless function. Hardware: a standard laptop. Built with help from Claude (Anthropic).

What’s creative about it:

  • It doesn’t stop at a corrected chart. It shows the doubt behind every estimate, proves the sensors agree at the level of individual detections, and turns the record into a forecast.
  • The pixel lab lets anyone see why one MODIS pixel becomes several VIIRS hotspots.
  • The haze outlook combines fire forecasts with wind direction.
  • The console design makes 25 years of data explorable in minutes.

Factors we considered:

  • Honesty: uncertainty bands, a forecast scored against a normal-year guess, and limits stated on the page. Counts are detections, not burned area; cloud and smoke hide fires; 2001 to mid-2002 is Terra only.
  • Security: the API key stays on the server.
  • Performance: detections are pre-aggregated into grid cells, and each sector loads only when picked.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-friendly colours, reduced motion, a mute switch.
  • Reproducibility: open code, and documented pipeline commands that rebuild every dataset.
